items.title: Declarations of Pecuniary Interest under the “Municipal Conflict of Interest Act”
Public Hearing of Development Charges Complaint under Subsection 20(4) of the “Development Charges Act”, 1997, as Amended
PDL-LEG-25-005, Development Charges Complaint - 162 Snyder’s Road East, Baden
notes:
Chair M. Harris provided an overview of the process for the hearing.

Richard Brookes, Senior Solicitor, provided an overview of the staff report. He noted that the Development Charges (DC) By-law includes a brownfield provision, allowing developers to obtain credits for Regional Development Charges (RDCs). In 2018, Council made a decision to phase out the brownfield development program within the by-law. He explained how the program functioned prior to its phase-out. He spoke to the development in question, and that it consists of a 23-unit residential complex, and the environmental remediation work occurred in 2021, noting that the issue at hand is whether the complainant met the deadline to qualify for the 100% RDC credit. As staff understand, the complainant’s position is that the certification of the Record of Site Condition (RSC) was submitted before January 1, 2022, and that the term "issued" in the by-law is not explicitly defined. Therefore, they argue that the certification date satisfies the requirement of being “issued” before January 1, 2022. He clarified that not every term in legislation is defined, and the staff report references a legal principle of statutory interpretation that applies in this case. R. Brookes outlined the available options for Council’s consideration.

The Committee inquired whether the development was already in progress when Council was considering changes to the policy. Janine Fletcher, Senior Planner, explained that Council was not aware of the development at that time and acknowledged that while the Ministry had confirmed receipt of the Record of Site Condition (RSC), this did not mean the RDC credit was approved and that approval is only granted on the date the Ministry formally confirms the site qualifies as a brownfield and is eligible for the credit.

The Committee discussed the interpretation of the by-law, the importance of meeting deadlines, the impact of provincial timelines and delays, and that making an exception in this case could set a precedent, potentially requiring the reopening of multiple files. R. Brookes provided clarification on the sequence of events and addressed related questions.

Chris Barnett, Osler, Hoskin & Harcourt LLP., provided an overview on behalf of 162 Snyder's Road and clarified the terminology used in the Environmental Protection Act regarding Records of Site Condition (RSC). He noted that the term "issued" is not explicitly defined in the legislation, and instead, terms such as "certified," "submitted," and "filed" are used. C. Barnett provided background on the applicant, highlighting that the company has been active in real estate development in Wilmot for 65 years and that the principal has played a significant role in the community, including the donation of a 14-acre property for a park. C. Barnett noted that the development site, previously home to a gas station, a meat market, and a landscaping business, had remained vacant after a fire in 2016, and to facilitate residential development, extensive remediation was undertaken at a cost of approximately $330,000, leading to the construction of a high-quality 32-unit rental apartment building. He spoke to the Brownfield Incentive Program, which was originally designed to promote compact growth, utilize existing infrastructure, mitigate groundwater risks, and increase tax revenue. He indicated that Council amended the policy in 2019, phasing out the program while allowing for a 50% development charge credit if an RSC was issued after January 1, 2022.

Sean Anderson, Senior Project Manager, responded to Committee members' inquiries regarding the submission dates to the ministry, and the clarification on the engineer's submission.

R. Brookes and C. Barnett made closing remarks. Committee members spoke to their positions.

N. Salonen requested that staff revise the language to prevent similar situations from arising.

items.title: Strategic Priority - Equitable Services and Opportunities
RSC-SPR-25-003, 2024 Accessibility Status Report
notes:
Connie MacDonald provided a presentation on the 2024 Accessibility Status Report. A copy of the presentation is appended to the original agenda. She outlined that the presentation will outline the accomplishments of 2024 and what is to come. Jennifer Walker, Program Manager, Resident Experience continued the presentation and spoke to the importance of accessibility, accessibility for Ontarians with Disabilities Act (AODA) and provided information on the act. 

Ryan Pettipiere, Director Housing Services continued the presentation speaking to the 2024 accomplishments, the Waterloo Region Housing Revitalization Plan (WRH RP) highlighting that this plan is prioritizing affordability, accessibility and energy efficiency.  Doug Spooner, Acting Commissioner, Transportation continued the presentation, providing highlights with Grant River Transit (GRT) with regards to accessibility, the upcoming 2025 launch of Neurons adaptive micromobility vehicles. 

J. Walker concluded the presentation speaking to the plans for 2025. 

Committee members inquired about the Grand River Accessibility Advisory Committee (GRAAC) membership, specifically regarding not only spatial disabilities but also other types, such as learning disabilities. J. Walker responded and clarified that while there has been a lot of focus on physical and mobility disabilities, they aim to shift this focus as they learn more about non-visible disabilities and continue to evolve. C. MacDonald further responded to questions regarding GRAAC noting that staff are collaborating with other municipalities, with the City of Kitchener currently serving as the administrative lead. It is up to Council to decide if they wish to delegate this responsibility differently.

D. Spooner addressed the road conditions and the difference between rural and urban standards, noting that these factors will be considered as the Township Transit Plan progresses.

R. Pettipiere responded to questions, confirming that the accessibility features and the number of units per building will be consistent across all unit sizes in the new developments.

This report was received for information.

items.title: PDL-CUL-25-004, Key Cultural Institutions 2025 Funding Allocations
notes:
Rod Regier, Commissioner Planning, Development & Legislative Services, spoke to the Key Cultural Institutions 2025 Funding Allocations. He noted the importance of the KCIs.

Julian Kingston, Director of Cultural Services, discussed the allocation and the report, outlining how the allocation can be approached for 2025. He provided a breakdown of the allocations.

In response to a question from the Committee, J. Kingston discussed whether work has been done based on the upper limit of criteria. He explained that when reviewing the financials of an organization, they do not stratify them based on financials, which results in differences between KCIs, particularly in terms of the higher and lower levels of their budgets. Initially, when the grants were established, the focus was on approximately 10 percent of the operating revenue level.

Staff were directed to explore the possibility of setting an upper limit criteria for organizations in need of funding. R. Regier confirmed they would take this as direction and mentioned that they have ongoing discussions with area municipalities regarding the criteria for evaluating key cultural institutions. The most recent evaluation took place in mid-2024, in preparation for the 2025 budget cycle. Staff will look into this matter and report back to the Committee. C. Huinink requested that this be added to the tracking list.

Committee members inquired about the difference in grants between Drayton Entertainment and THEMUSEUM. J. Kingston responded, explaining that the grant allocations have remained consistent, with the same amounts allocated as in previous years. Referring to the 10 percent rule of thumb, he noted that Drayton Entertainment would absorb a significant portion of the total grant allocation, potentially taking up more than the entire grant when distributed across the KCIs.

The report was received for information.

items.title: COR-CFN-25-001, 2025 Budget – Final Adjustments to Address Council Approved Motion Regarding Budget Reductions
notes:
Wayne Steffler, Commissioner Corporate Services/Chief Financial Officer, spoke to the 2025 Budget Final Adjustments to Address Council Approved Motion Regarding Budget Reductions. 

The Committee first addressed the levy-impacting items, followed by a discussion of the gross items that are not levy-impacting.

Responding to a question from the Committee regarding conferences, W. Steffler noted that the motion aimed to address increases in various accounts related to specific types of travel. However, the most significant cost increases were not in those areas. Instead, the focus was on identifying where costs were rising and exploring ways to reduce the overall increase.

J. Erb proposed an amendment to remove the funding reduction for encampment security. The amendment was carried.

Direction was given to staff to return with a proposal to replace the $349,766 for the amended encampment item.

D. Spooner addressed a Committee question by first noting that the approved GRT service package for 2025 was smaller than initially proposed, which allows for the retirement of older buses, specifically those from 2008 and 2009, which require more maintenance and consume additional parts. As a result, there is confidence in the budget allocation for bus parts. Regarding road salt, he indicated that a five-year review of spending was conducted to inform the budget. However, this analysis did not account for the severe winter conditions experienced in January and February. While this presents a potential budget risk, there will be no reduction in salt usage, and road maintenance will be fully maintained.

items.title: Regional Chair K. Redman Notice of Motion
notes:
Regional Chair K. Redman spoke to her motion, highlighting the strength of the Regional economy while emphasizing the need for proactive measures to address potential U.S. tariffs on Canadian goods. Given the Region’s strong reliance on manufacturing and exports, she indicated that a 25% tariff could significantly impact local businesses, jobs, and supply chains and in order to mitigate these risks, the motion outlines three key actions including exploring ways to limit the impact on regional services, reviewing procurement to prioritize Canadian-made goods, and working with economic development partners to develop a regional action plan. She stressed that acting now is crucial to protecting the region’s economy, strengthening local supply chains, and ensuring long-term economic resilience.

Members of the Committee deliberated on the motion.

N. Salonen suggested that the word 'agriculture' be added to the last paragraph to reflect not only the manufacturing impact but also agricultural impacts. K. Redman agreed to this suggestion.

Regional Chair K. Redman Notice of Motion
motions.text: WHEREAS Waterloo Region is home to a diverse economy WHEREAS The United States government has indicated a potential 25% tariff on Canadian made goods as of March 2025 WHEREAS Manufacturing in Waterloo Region is estimated to represent approximately 20% of our Gross Domestic Product and between 15-17% of our total workforce WHEREAS in 2023, exports from all Waterloo Region businesses reached $19.4-billion, with 97% - or $18.9-billion - from manufacturing businesses. WHEREAS as of November 2024, 77% of all domestic exports from Ontario businesses went to the United States THEREFORE BE IT RESOLVED that Region of Waterloo staff explore options for limiting the impact of the potential United States’ sanctioned tariffs on Regional Services; and that Region of Waterloo staff review our current procurement process for opportunities to increase and/or demand made in Canada provisions; and that The Region of Waterloo formally requests the Waterloo Economic Development Corporation (WEDC), through the Business Economic Support Team Waterloo Region (BEST WR), develop an action plan to support Waterloo Region businesses, including those in the agricultural industry, and our collective economic interest.
motions.text_html:
WHEREAS Waterloo Region is home to a diverse economy
 
WHEREAS The United States government has indicated a potential 25% tariff on Canadian made goods as of March 2025 
 
WHEREAS Manufacturing in Waterloo Region is estimated to represent approximately 20% of our Gross Domestic Product and between 15-17% of our total workforce
 
WHEREAS in 2023, exports from all Waterloo Region businesses reached $19.4-billion, with 97% - or $18.9-billion - from manufacturing businesses.
 
WHEREAS as of November 2024, 77% of all domestic exports from Ontario businesses went to the United States 
 
THEREFORE BE IT RESOLVED that Region of Waterloo staff explore options for limiting the impact of the potential United States’ sanctioned tariffs on Regional Services; and that 
 
Region of Waterloo staff review our current procurement process for opportunities to increase and/or demand made in Canada provisions; and that
 
The Region of Waterloo formally requests the Waterloo Economic Development Corporation (WEDC), through the Business Economic Support Team Waterloo Region (BEST WR), develop an action plan to support Waterloo Region businesses, including those in the agricultural industry, and our collective economic interest.
